practice.title: Respect Others
agreedSteps: Practice prostration and respecting others over the next two weeks. Key in to people's sufferings and problems — view their struggles as important, more important than our own. Respect the unseen battles people are fighting every day.

When we have difficulty respecting someone, recognize that our self-cherishing is what prevents us from respecting them. Dissolve the 'inherently unrespectable person' we normally see — they don't exist.
View difficult people as our teachers. They are specifically training us for something — teaching us to have the courage to stand up to bad behavior when needed, while still respecting the person.
steps: Try making a mental prostration at any point in the day — on the train, lying down, wherever. It can be as simple as thinking: I prostrate to the Buddhas, with the goal of destroying self-cherishing or gaining humility.

Every time we see a Buddha image — at the gompa, at home, at our shrine — practice prostrating. Even just a subtle gesture. It's a great mindfulness practice and will increase our ability to remember Dharma throughout our daily life.
Recite this verse as a mantra before talking to someone: 'Whenever I associate with you, may I view myself as the lowest of all. With a pure intention, cherish you as supreme.'
practice.quote: To prostrate means to respect others. How much do I respect others, and what does it mean to really respect someone? Not just be with someone, not just be nice to someone, but to respect them.

commentary.title: What Problem Does Prostration Solve?
content: Just as with every practice we've looked at, the question to ask is: what is the problem that prostration will solve for us? There are several. We might have lots of non-virtue that needs purifying — prostration has great power to purify non-virtue. We might need positive meritorious energy — prostration accumulates that. We might have a false sense of pride — prostration develops humility. We might lack faith or respect for our spiritual guide — the prostration form plants seeds for that.

Whether prostration actually works depends solely on our mind. If we approach it with a pure motivation — wishing to overcome pride and keeping the qualities of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha uppermost in our mind — beneficial effects will definitely follow. A 'pure motivation' doesn't mean perfect focus. It just means some spiritual component — not treating it purely as a workout.

commentary.title: Three Types of Prostration
content: Shantideva mentions two types of prostration — verbal and physical — and other texts add a third: mental prostration, which is the attitude of respect and faith we extend toward worthy objects. Of these three, the most important is mental prostration. Faith is the root of all good qualities and all spiritual attainments. In the most beneficial form of practice, all three are performed simultaneously.

For physical prostrations, there are two methods in common use: the half-length prostration (kneeling, touching hands and forehead to the ground) and the full-length prostration (whole outstretched body in contact with the ground). But merely holding our hands at our heart, or even bowing our head slightly, qualifies as a physical prostration. It's not necessary to touch the ground at all.

There comes a point in every single person's life where holding their hands at their heart is the only way they can physically prostrate anymore. That point will come for all of us. But it's not deficient in any way — it's a completely perfect prostration. When we can't do the half-length or full-length, it's actually a privilege in some ways. It gives us the freedom to really do the mental part well — imagining infinite bodies prostrating for infinite eons. We can let our imagination go wild.

commentary.title: The Four-Point Touch
content: We place the palms of our hands together with thumbs tucked inside, symbolizing a wish-fulfilling jewel, and touch our folded hands to four places: the top of our head — to attain a Buddha's ushnisha, planting seeds for faith and respect for our spiritual guide. The forehead — a sign of wisdom, solving our ignorance problem. The throat — power of speech. The heart — power of mind. If our motivation and faith are strong, these practices place powerful potentialities in our mindstream for a Buddha's transcendent body, speech, and mind.

The tradition is that the four-point touch goes with the half-length and full-length prostrations. When just holding our hands at our heart, we don't need to do the four-point touch. A friend said she thinks during prostrations, 'May I be like the rug underneath your feet' — offensive to our self-cherishing mind, but a beautiful attitude of humility.

commentary.title: Making Prostration Vast
content: The true value of prostration depends on our mental attitude. If we visualize our body appearing in numberless manifestations, all making prostrations to infinite Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, we will receive benefits as great as our visualization is vast. The same three qualities we applied to offerings work here too: remembering the reasoning and benefit, making it vast and infinite, and feeling the Buddhas' delight.

Start with a benchmark — can I imagine 100,000 bodies prostrating in a huge stadium? Then fill all of New York City, then the whole country, the solar system, a galaxy. Impute that it's for countless eons too, because time is imputed. It's nice to make Buddhas prostrating to Buddhas — your Vajrayogini bodies are prostrating, or your Heruka bodies.

Naropa used prostrations as his chief external method for accumulating merit. Je Tsongkhapa performed three and a half million full-length prostrations, famously eroding a ditch in the ground. In Tibet it was common for laypeople to prostrate the entire distance around Lhasa, or all the way from eastern Tibet to Kailash Mountain — a journey that normally took six months by foot. This is still going on today.

commentary.title: Respecting the Sacred
content: It's a key human awareness to view things as sacred. The sacred and the profane are at odds — what is profane is not sacred. It's okay to make jokes about things, but we need to be aware when something is beyond even something we would joke about, because it's so holy. It's protective of our mind to think, that's beyond anything I would even joke about. It's so special.

It's like why we don't wear hats in the gompa, or why we take our shoes off. These aren't rules — they're mind protection. They're scaffolding to help us train in making something feel separate and apart, sacred and holy. One extreme is viewing them as strange rules to enforce on others. The other extreme is to forgo them utterly, thinking they're superstitious. Buddhism is beyond both — these structures help our mind, and they help a tradition pass on generation after generation.

A simple way to grow respect for Buddhas: every time we see a Buddha image — at the gompa, at home, at our shrine — practice prostrating. Even just subtly. If you see any videos of Geshe-la walking in to teach, every single time he prostrates to the Buddhas. Every single 100% of the time. It's completely ingrained in his mind's machinery. If we practice this, we'll become mindfulness machines. The whole space will feel sacred and magical.

commentary.title: Respect for Living Beings — 'Lowest of All'
content: With the people of our life — family, friends, co-workers, Sangha friends — we want to ask: how much do I really respect them? Not tolerate, not be outwardly nice to while looking down on them. We can be nice to someone while giving them a little pity. That's not respect. We want to key in on the difference — how does it feel when we're really respecting someone versus just tolerating them?

There are two ways into respect, like two sides of a seesaw. One is to view ourselves as the lowest of all, the other is to view others as supreme. Lowering us raises them, raising them lowers us. The verse from Eight Steps to Happiness: 'Whenever I associate with others, may I view myself as the lowest of all. With a pure intention, may I cherish others as supreme.' We can personalize it: 'Whenever I associate with you, may I view myself as the lowest of all. With a pure intention, cherish you as supreme.' Recite it as a mantra before a phone call, a meeting, a coffee date.

commentary.title: Humility Is Relief, Not Self-Deprecation
content: Three reasons to practice humility: first, we're not using up our merit on worldly attainment — we're saving it for internal realizations. Second, by wishing for others to enjoy higher status, we accumulate a vast amount of merit. Third, there is no self that we normally see — there's no reason to be proud about a non-existent. And anyone could be a Buddha, like in the story of Asanga and Maitreya with the dog.

A humble mind is a mega-blessed mind. Just as water can't collect on mountain peaks, good qualities and blessings can't gather on the rocky peaks of pride. If we maintain a humble attitude, good qualities and inspiration will flow into our mind like streams flowing into a valley. Many people experience this when they hit rock bottom — they shed all the pretension and get a Cambrian explosion of growth, totally open to everyone and everything.

'Lowest of all' is like a self-generation practice — instead of thinking 'I am Buddha,' we impute 'lowest of all' as our label. The corresponding feeling is freakish levels of relief. Just incredible relief. If the feeling we're getting is self-deprecation or self-criticism or low self-esteem, that means we missed the boat. Those minds are actually pride. The practice should feel like putting down an enormous burden. One way in: identify as Vajrayogini. Think, I'm not wishing for the self I normally see to be happy. Because that self doesn't exist. And notice the relief.
commentary.quote: If we try to practice this and the feeling we're getting is self-deprecation or self-criticism or low self-esteem, that means we didn't really get it right. Those minds are pride. The corresponding feeling is freakish levels of relief.

commentary.title: The Four Intervention Points
content: There are only a few intervention points where we can make things move in our mind. Think upstream, downstream. The compound minds — love, compassion, respect — are at the pool at the bottom of a waterfall. At the top there are just four little spouts: attention, discrimination (how we label things), intention, and mindfulness (what we're remembering). We have to turn on one of those spouts to get things moving.

A lot of times we get into trouble because we're standing at the bottom of the pool going, 'Where's the love? Where's the compassion? Go away, delusions!' When really we need to trot up to the top of the waterfall and work on those spouts. Relabeling — calling everyone 'friend' — is working the discrimination spout. Even if you don't mean it at first. Do it over and over and the water will flow.
commentary.quote: A lot of times we get into trouble because we're standing at the bottom of the pool going, where's the love? Where's the compassion? What we really need to do is trot up to the top of the waterfall and start working on some of those spouts.
